CAMPUS INFORMATION Student Drop-off/pick-up info UPDATE TO STUDENT CHECKOUTS In order to serve our Ranger Families best, we are implementing a cutoff time for students to be checked out. Starting on 11/11/24, all in-person checkouts need to occur BEFORE 2:45 PM. Please anticipate a 20 minute wait. Due to construction on campus, several areas are closed resulting in longer times to deliver early dismissal passes to classrooms and longer times for students to walk from their classrooms to the front office. After 2:45 PM, please wait to meet your student at the
label: Vista Ridge High School

text: Vista Ridge High School. normal dismissal time. Our recommendation: 1) send a parent note with your student in the morning for them to bring to the Attendance Office before school or 2) send an email by 10:30 AM to vrhsearlydismissal@leanderisd.org so that an Early Dismissal pass can be given to your student prior to his/her desired dismissal time. This means you will avoid having to wait in line for a pass to be sent to your student and that they can simply meet you in the front of the school at the desired time–you won’t even have to step foot in the building! In conclusion: Send a parent note with your student in the morning for them to bring to the Attendance Office before school or send an email to vrhsearlydismissal@leanderisd.org by 10:30 AM so that an Early Dismissal pass can be given to your student prior to his/her desired dismissal time. Early dismissal
label: Vista Ridge High School

text: Vista Ridge High School. notes/emails that are received by 10:30 AM with a dismissal time later than 2:45 PM will still be accepted. The 2:45 PM cutoff time is simply for in-person checkouts. Please be advised that any attempt to check out a student during his/her lunch or athletic period could result in a longer wait or possibly an unsuccessful location of the student. On early release days (12/ 19 /2 5 & 5/2 9 /2 6 ) the cutoff pickup time will be 11:45 AM . Thank you for your patience and understanding. Go Rangers! text: Hours Owed. my student owe hours? Any student who does not attend 90% of the days a class is offered (excused or unexcused) will be required to make-up attendance hours. Hours are calculated by class, by semester. A student cannot miss a class period more than four times per semester. Once a student misses their 5th class period, they owe 1.5 hours for every additional missed class. The following attendance codes generate hours owed: A (Absence-Excused) D (Absence w/Doctor Note-full day) O (Unverified-Unexcused) U (Unexcused) TA (Late to Class, Absent) What is the difference between owing hours and truancy? Owing hours determines whether or not a student received credit for their courses. Truancy determines whether or not a student is meeting the required attendance laws. text: Hours Owed. hours owed. How does my student Make up hours? Hours can be made up by: Attending AM or PM Study Halls Attending Saturday School Attendance hours need to be documented on the [Attendance Hours Tracking Form](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1eI-X1hNFmoOk950AzDEihX01TWFFg-eL/view?usp=sharing) . (Forms can also be found in the AP office) Completed forms can be turned in to Joanna Norling or Micah Gillum in the Assistant Principal's office How do I request an appeal? VRHS has an hours owed appeals committee that meets regularly. If your student owes hours for any special circumstances (ie. medical procedures/surgery, etc.), please contact your [assistant principal](https://sites.google.com/leanderisd.org/vrhs-assistant-principals-offi/home) to discuss the process and request an appeals form. label: VRHS Attendance - Student Sign Out

VRHS Attendance - Absences ABSENCES Documentation for Student Absences As stated in the LISD Handbook, d ocumentation for absences should be received within 2 days after the student returns to school . All student absences must be verified in writing with a parent note/email, medical note or other state approved document. Changes cannot be made to absences in previous grading cycles with parent notes. Up to 20 parent notes will be accepted for excused absences per school year. Medical notes and other state approved documentation are always accepted. Phone calls are not permitted as documentation for any absence. label: VRHS Attendance - Absences

text: VRHS Attendance - Tardies. VRHS Attendance - Tardies TARDIES Tardies Students must be present in 1st/5th period when the 8:15 bell rings. If a student arrives to ANY class within 10 minutes of bell ringing, they are counted tardy. If a student arrives to ANY class AFTER 10 minutes of bell ringing, they are counted absent for that period. Assistant Principals are monitoring tardies - excessive tardies could result in consequences. If a student arrives after the start of school they must check in at the attendance office. This includes passing periods, Ranger Time and lunch .
label: VRHS Attendance - Tardies

text: VRHS Attendance - College Visits. VRHS Attendance - College Visits COLLEGE VISITS College Visits Juniors and Seniors are allowed 2 college visit days per school year. Official verification of the visit from the institution of higher education must be provided within 2 days of the student's return to VRHS. Per TEA Guidelines we cannot accept pre-tour confirmation emails, maps, name tags, parking permits, itineraries, or pictures of your student, etc. as official documentation. Verification of the official college visit MUST be on college letterhead and include the student's first and last name, and date of the visit; it can be emailed to VRHSattendance@leanderisd.org
label: VRHS Attendance - College Visits

text: VRHS Attendance - Hours Owed. VRHS Attendance - Hours Owed HOURS OWED General Information Any student who does not attend 90% of the days a class is offered (excused or unexcused) will be required to make-up attendance hours. Hours are calculated by class, by semester. A student cannot miss a class period more than four times per semester. Once a student misses their 5th class period, they owe 1.5 hours for every additional missed class. The following attendance codes generate hours owed: A (Absence-Excused) D (Absence w/Doctor Note-full day) O (Unverified-Unexcused) U (Unexcused) TA (Late to Class, Absent) What is the difference between owing hours and truancy? Owing hours determines whether or not a
label: VRHS Attendance - Hours Owed

text: VRHS Attendance - Hours Owed. student received credit for their courses. Truancy determines whether or not a student is meeting the required attendance laws. For additional information, please visit the [Hours Owed](https://vrhs.leanderisd.org/campus_information/hours-owed) webpage. Please contact your [Assistant Principa](https://sites.google.com/leanderisd.org/vrhs-assistant-principals-offi/home) l if you have any questions.
label: VRHS Attendance - Hours Owed

Reach A reach school for you would be a school in which your SAT or ACT score is lower than the average score range of last year's freshman class. VRHS COUNSELING - Apprenticeship/Trade School Apprenticeships & Trades For many high school graduates that are interested in joining the work force in a skilled labor job, apprenticeships are an amazing opportunity to get training while earning a high wage. Learning by Doing: Apprenticeships are known for their hands-on approach, where learners directly apply their knowledge in a real work environment. Combines Training with Work: Apprenticeships include both practical, job-related training and theoretical classroom education. Industry-Driven: Apprenticeships are often created with the needs of specific industries in mind, ensuring that apprentices develop the skills required for those industries. Mentorship: Apprentices often work under the guidance
label: VRHS COUNSELING - Apprenticeship/Trade School

text: VRHS COUNSELING - Apprenticeship/Trade School. of a mentor, a skilled professional in the field, who provides support and guidance. Wage Increases: Apprenticeships can offer a pathway to a higher-paying job through skill development and experience gained during the apprenticeship. Nationally-Recognized Credentials: Successful completion of a Registered Apprenticeship program can lead to a portable, nationally-recognized credential. Benefits: Earning a wage while gaining skills and experience, rather than accumulating student debt. Developing in-demand skills that lead to good-paying jobs. Receiving hands-on training and mentoring from experienced professionals. Apprenticeship Levels: Apprenticeships can be classified as Intermediate, Advanced, Higher, and Degree Apprenticeships. Apprenticeship Durations: Apprenticeships can last from 1-4 years, depending on the occupation. Four years is common for most professional trade occupations but shorter apprenticeships are becoming popular. text: DISTANCE LEARNING. DISTANCE LEARNING Dual Credit Resources Distance Education WHAT IS DISTANCE LEARNING? Distance Learning is the term ACC uses for courses offered in an online format. This format gives students more scheduling options and a wider selection of classes to meet individual needs. Meanwhile, course content and transferability is
label: Vista Ridge College & Career Center - DISTANCE LEARNING

text: DISTANCE LEARNING. identical to classes offered on campus and in-person. As with all ACC courses, there is a defined start and end date and professors will still dictate due dates/deadlines. SYNCHRONOUS VS. ASYNCHRONOUS DISTANCE LEARNING (DIL) If a DIL course does not indicate meeting times, the course will be conducted fully asynchronous, meaning there are no class meetings. Typical DIL courses require students to review the syllabus and complete an initial online orientation, then access course materials typically via Blackboard. Students may be required to read text, complete study guides, participate in discussion boards, research, write papers, develop presentations, etc. If a DIL course does indicate meeting times, the professor will hold synchronous class meetings to deliver instruction. Again, course materials will typically be pushed out via Blackboard, yet the course will be conducted in a much more traditional fashion, but virtually. TIPS FOR SUCCESS IN DISTANCE LEARNING CLASSES 1. Prep your
label: Vista Ridge College & Career Center - DISTANCE LEARNING

text: DISTANCE LEARNING. technology. You will need a computer, web access, and in some cases a web cam or headphones. Keep these items charged, ready to go. 2. Dedicate time for your course. Carve out structured time specifically allotted to dedicate to each of your online courses. This could be every day, every Mon/Wed, mornings, evenings...think about when you work best and are most focused. 3. Choose a workspace. Find a place that is free of distractions (siblings, TV, etc.) and comfortable where you can stay focused. Find a desk, dining room table, etc. - couches and beds may be your productivity nemesis! 4. Use your online tools. Check [Blackboard](https://acconline.austincc.edu/) (for your coursework and grades) and your [ACCemail](https://www.austincc.edu/help/accmail) regularly. This is how professors will communicate with you. 5. Team up! There is power in accountability. Connect with other students in your class to check-in, discuss learning, or study together. 6. Plan & organize.

text: TSI. TSI TEXAS SUCCESS INITIATIVE (TSI) TSI stands for Texas Success Initiative and is the standard by which Texas public post-secondary institutions evaluate a student's college readiness in reading, writing, and math. In a nutshell, if a student is not "TSI complete," the college will assume a student is
label: Vista Ridge College & Career Center - TSI

text: TSI. not ready to take on college-level coursework. In turn, the college will require the student to take developmental coursework to build knowledge and skills. This required developmental coursework costs money and prevents students from jumping right into courses that will apply toward the completion of a college degree. If we can avoid this coursework by proving students are TSI complete, we most certainly want to! The TSI can be met with a student's SAT, ACT, or TSI scores. If a student met the TSI with their SAT or ACT, that student would request their scores to be sent from the College Board or ACT website. ACC has a comprehensive [TSI test prep site](http://sites.austincc.edu/tsiprep/) with practice tests and review College Board [FREE web-based study app](https://practice.accuplacer.org/login) College Board [sample questions](https://accuplacer.collegeboard.org/students/prepare-for-accuplacer/practice) (Accuplacer and Texas' TSI) [Sample essays & scores](https://secure-media.collegeboard.org/digitalServices/pdf/accuplacer/accuplacer-tsi-writeplacer-sample-essays.pdf) Learning Express - [free TSI practice tests](https://www.learningexpresshub.com/productengine/LELIndex.html#/prepstephighschool/staarprep/resources/tsi-placement-test-preparation-cat/tsi-placement-test-preparation-subcat/tsi-placement-test-preparation) [Mometrix Test Prep](https://www.mometrix.com/academy/tsi-test/) What if I fail the test? Rather than stress the singular goal of competition preparation, lessons emphasize on nurturing independence and individual skills critical to the developing singer. text: Vista Ridge Theatre - International Thespians Society. Vista Ridge Theatre - International Thespians Society What is International Thespian Society? International Thespian Society (ITS) is a theatre based honor society. Membership is granted through a point system based on performance, work ethic, and time spent doing theatre arts that meets the Society's guidelines. What Are Thespian Points? Thespian Points is a point system to track student performance, and allow students to be inducted into the Society. Each thespian needs a minimum of 10 points to be inducted, but can recieve higher honors by gaining more points. What are Thespian Inductions? Theatre students who gain 10 Thespian points based on after-school participation for their respective Theatre Department (about 10 hours per point) qualify to be inducted into the International Thespian Society. What do Students Get? An official membership

text: About Us. Welcome! PTA is a grassroots organization made up of parents, teachers and others around the state who have a special interest in children, families and schools. PTA membership is as diverse as Texas is in cultures, education levels and parenting skills. By joining PTA, a member automatically becomes part of the largest child-advocacy organization in the state -- over 630,000 strong across Texas. PTA's MISSION The mission of the PTA is three-fold: To support and speak on behalf of children and youth in the schools, in the community and before governmental bodies and other organizations that make decisions affecting children; To assist parents in developing the skills they need to raise and protect their children; and To encourage parent and public involvement in the public schools of this nation. THE PURPOSE OF PTA To promote the welfare of children and youth in home, school, community and place of worship; To
label: Vista Ridge LISD PTSA - About Us

text: About Us. raise the standards of home life; To secure adequate laws for the care and protection of children and youth; To bring into closer relation the home and the school, that parents and teachers may cooperate intelligently in the education of children and youth; To develop between educators and the general public such united efforts as will secure for all children and youth the highest advantages in physical, mental, social and spiritual education. WHAT DOES PTA DO? PTAs work for children. PTAs meet together, study problems, support teachers, volunteer in schools, attend workshops on parenting and become informed on issues regarding children and youth. As a result, PTA members become better parents, teachers and citizens. WHY JOIN THE PTA? Being an active PTA member has many advantages: It is a great way to become familiar with the teachers and the school. It allows you to have some influence over how money

label: Hours Owed

text: Hours Owed. the days a class is offered (excused or unexcused) will be required to make-up attendance hours. Hours are calculated by class, by semester. A student cannot miss a class period more than four times per semester. Once a student misses their 5th class period, they owe 1.5 hours for every additional missed class. The following attendance codes generate hours owed: A (Absence-Excused) D (Absence w/Doctor Note-full day) O (Unverified-Unexcused) U (Unexcused) TA (Late to Class, Absent) What is the difference between owing hours and truancy? Owing hours determines whether or not a student received credit for their courses. Truancy determines whether or not a student is meeting the required attendance laws. Where can I go to check if my student owes hours? You can reach out to Joanna Norling or Micah Gillum in the AP office for your hours owed. How does my student Make up hours? Hours can be
label: Hours Owed

text: Hours Owed. made up by: Attending AM or PM Study Halls Attending Saturday School Attendance hours need to be documented on the [Attendance Hours Tracking Form](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1eI-X1hNFmoOk950AzDEihX01TWFFg-eL/view?usp=sharing) . (Forms can also be found in the AP office) Completed forms can be turned in to Joanna Norling or Micah Gillum in the Assistant Principal's office How do I request an appeal? VRHS has an hours owed appeals committee that meets regularly. If your student owes hours for any special circumstances (ie. medical procedures/surgery, etc.), please contact your [assistant principal](https://sites.google.com/leanderisd.org/vrhs-assistant-principals-offi/home) to discuss the process and request an appeals form. Please contact your [Assistant Principal](https://sites.google.com/leanderisd.org/vrhs-assistant-principals-offi/home?authuser=0) with any questions.

text: Ms. Way. Ms. Way ABOUT MS.WAY Julianne Way is entering her tenth year of teaching as the Assistant Dance Director at VRHS and of the Star Steppers and Rubies JV Dance Team. Julianne was raised in Cedar Park, Texas where she attended elementary, middle, and high school in the Leander Independent School District. She attended Vista Ridge High School and was a member of the Star Stepper Dance Team for 3 years and held the position of Captain her senior year. Following her time at Vista Ridge, Julianne attended Texas State University in San Marcos, Texas. During her time at Texas State she was a member of the Strutters Dance Team and held the position of Senior Captain her 4th year on the
label: Ms. Way

text: Ms. Way. team. Julianne graduated from Texas State with a BFA in Dance Education. In addition to teaching at Vista Ridge, Julianne is also a teacher and choreographer for many dance teams at various levels in the state of Texas and for many years was a staff member with ShowMakers of America, a dance company that hosts summer camps and contests. Ms. Way is looking forward to her tenth year of teaching Dance I, Studio Dance 1, Rubies, Starline, Star Steppers and being part of her alma mater! Classes: Star Steppers- 1st and 5th Period JV Dance- 2nd Period Studio Dance I- 3rd Period Drill Team Prep- 6th Period Dance 1- 7th Period Conference- 4th and 8th period Contact Info: julianne.way@leanderisd.org Room #3207 Phone: 512-570-1870 Conference: 2:05pm-3:35pm (Everyday)

text: mLISD Empowered Learning - Technology Application TEKS. mLISD Empowered Learning - Technology Application TEKS Technology Integration: There are TEKS for that! last updated: August 2025 Why Integrate Technology? In today’s dynamic classrooms, technology serves as a bridge between core content instruction and real-world application, aligning seamlessly with the Texas Technology Application TEKS. By integrating technology, teachers are not adding complexity; they are enhancing teaching. For instance, digital simulations can transform a science lesson on ecosystems into an interactive experience, while collaborative tools empower students to present their findings in new and interesting way.
label: mLISD Empowered Learning - Technology Application TEKS

text: mLISD Empowered Learning - Technology Application TEKS. Technology integration enriches lessons without requiring an overhaul. Many educators worry about technology increasing their workload, but TEKS-aligned tools are designed to simplify instruction. These tools support differentiation, ensuring all students engage deeply with the material while making lessons more accessible and engaging. By aligning your teaching with Texas Technology Application TEKS, you create vibrant, student-centered classrooms that inspire curiosity and foster essential skills for lifelong learning. TEKS [TEA Introduction to Technology Applications](https://d1yqpar94jqbqm.cloudfront.net/documents/Introduction%20PDF%20for%20TEKS%20Guide%20-%20Tech%20Apps.pdf) TechApps Vertical Alignment.pdf The Texas State Board of Education (SBOE) adopted new standards for Technology Applications in 2022. These standards are to be implemented by school districts beginning with the 2024 - 2025 school year. WeTeach_CS (UT) has compiled these standards into a vertical alignment document [here](https://utakeit.tacc.utexas.edu/resources/K8TechAppsTEKS_VerticalAlignment_22/) . text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's FAQ's What does IDEA stand for? The I ndividuals with D isabilities E ducation A ct of 2004 is the federal law that governs the special education process. What does FAPE stand for? One of the main purposes of IDEA is to ensure that children with disabilities have available to them a F ree A ppropriate P ublic E ducation (FAPE) that emphasizes special education and related services designed to meet their unique needs and prepare them for further education, employment, and independent living. What are Special Education and Related Services? Special Education refers to specially designed instruction to meet the unique needs of a
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. child with a disability. Related Services are special services needed to support students' special education services so they can make progress to meet their academic and functional goals. These services can include: occupational therapy, physical therapy, speech-language therapy, counseling services, orientation and mobility services, and/or transportation services. What is the ARD Committee or IEP Team and what does it do? After an initial evaluation report is completed on a student, the A dmission, R eview and D ismissal ( ARD ) Committee, also referred to as an I ndividualized E ducation P rogram ( IEP ) Team, must be formed to review the report and determine whether or not the student is eligible for special education services. Who is on the ARD/IEP Team? ARD/IEP committee members include the following: Parent/legal guardian or surrogate parent At least one special education teacher or service provider At least one general education teacher School
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. representative or administrator An individual who can interpret instructional implications of evaluation results Student, when appropriate, including when transition services are discussed Other individuals who have knowledge of the student Representatives of any participating agency potentially responsible for providing transition services, as appropriate Others for specific situations, such as a member of the Language Proficiency Assessment Committee (LPAC), a representative of Career and Technology Education (CTE) when considering CTE classes, or a teacher certified in the education for visual or auditory impairment How will I know about my student's ARD meetings? We will contact you via phone call or email to schedule meetings as far in advance as possible so you can request time off or make the necessary arrangements to attend the meeting. You will also receive written notice of the meeting at least five school days before the meeting, unless you agree to a shorter timeframe. The notice
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. will include the purpose, time, location and a list of those who will be in attendance. What if I can't physically attend the meeting? We understand everyone's situation is different. If you are unable to attend the meeting in person, you can participate through alternative means such as through telephone or videoconferencing. What is an IEP? If a student qualifies for special education services, the school is required to provide a Free Appropriate Public Education in the least restrictive environment. This is accomplished through the ARD committee's development of an I ndividualized E ducation P rogram ( IEP ) and the school's implementation of that IEP. The major components of the IEP include: The student's present levels of academic achievement and functional performance (PLAAFP); This includes how the student's disability affects involvement and progress in the general curriculum Annual goals; These goals are measurable annual goals designed to meet the
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. student's needs resulting from the disability so that he or she can be involved in and progress in the general curriculum. The IEP must also describe how the student's progress towards the annual goals will be measured as well as when the progress reports will be provided to parents. Description of the special education, related services, supplementary aids and services that will be provided; The ARD Committee will decide what services are needed to enable the student to: advance appropriate towards attaining the annual goals; be involved and make progress in the general curriculum; and be educated and participate with children without disabilities. The IEP must also include a statement of any needed program modifications and supports for school personnel that will be provided as well as the projected date for the beginning of the services and modifications and the anticipated frequency, location, and duration of the services and modifications.
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. Information regarding how the student will participate in state and district assessments; Transition services, when age-appropriate; and IDEA and state law require that IEPs for older students address transition services. These services are a coordinated set of activities designed to help the student move from school to post-school activities. Transition planning must begin no later than when a student reaches 14 years of age. The first IEP in effect when a student turns 16, must include appropriate measurable post-secondary goals based on age-appropriate transition assessments related to training, education, employment, and where appropriate, independent living skills. Your student must be invited to the ARD Committee meeting when transition services will be discussed. HOWEVER... If the ARD Committee determines that accommodations are necessary for a student to participate in assessments, the IEP must contain a statement of the appropriate accommodations. If the ARD Committee determines that a student must take an alternate assessment instead of a particular state or district wide assessment, statements must be provided regarding why the student cannot participate in the regular assessment and why the particular alternate assessment selected is appropriate for the student. What happens when my student turns 18? When your student reaches the age of 18, they become an adult student. These students have the right to make decisions on their own behalf unless determined by law to be incompetent. In the ARD Committee meeting held at least one
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

Additional information and resources regarding guardianship, alternatives to guardianship and information about other supports and services designed to assist in independent living will also be shared with students and parents. Please note, when your rights transfer to your adult student, you and your adult student will both receive all future required notices. However, notices of ARD Committee meetings are not an invitation for you to attend the meetings. You may only attend meetings if your adult student invites you or gives the school permission to invite you. What is a BIP? label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. part of your student's IEP. What does Placement mean? IDEA requires that a student with a disability be educated in the least restrictive environment (also referred to as the LRE). This means that a student must be educated with children who do not have disabilities to the maximum extent possible. Placement refers to the points along the continuum of placement options available for a student with a disability (i.e. regular classes, special classes, special schools, homebound instruction, instruction in hospitals and institutions). Placement does not refer to the specific physical location or site where the services will be delivered. What if I don't agree with the ARD Committee decision? You will be offered a single opportunity to have the Committee recess for a period of time not to exceed 10 school days unless you and the school mutually agree otherwise. During this recess time, the members of the Committee must
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. consider alternatives, gather additional information, prepare further documentation, and/or obtain additional resource persons who may assist in enabling the ARD Committee to reach mutual agreement. Do I get a copy of my student's IEP? Yes, the school must provide you with a copy of your student's IEP at no cost. If your native language is not English, we will strive to provide you with a written copy or audio-recording of your student's IEP translated into your native language. How often do we meet or review the IEP? Except for special circumstance, the ARD Committee will meet at least once a year to review your student's IEP and determine whether or not the annual goals are being met. You may request an ARD Committee meeting to discuss educational concerns about your child. Special circumstances which may require the ARD Committee to meet more than once include the need to address: Lack
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. of expected progress towards the annual goals and in the general curriculum; Results of any reevaluation; Information about the child provided to, or by, the parents; Anticipated needs of the child; or Other matters. Some changes to the IEP may be made without holding an ARD Committee meeting. However, the following changes can only be made in an ARD Committee meeting: Changes to eligibility determination; Changes in placement; and Manifestation determinations How often are students reevaluated for services? At least every three years the school will complete a reevaluation similar to the initial evaluation. This reevaluation must be comprehensive enough to determine whether or not your student continues to be a student with a disability and needs special education services. As part of the reevaluation process, the school will perform a R eview of E xisting E valuation D ata ( REED ). What if I want to revoke services?
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

text: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's. Just as you have the authority to consent to the initial provision of special education and related services, you have the authority to revoke your consent for services. Revocation of services must be made in writing. Once the school receives your written revocation, we will provide you with prior written notice that services will stop prior to discontinuing services. Special education and related services will be stopped; however, your student's education records will not be amended and references to your student's previous special education and related services in the past will not be removed. Please note, if you revoke your consent for the continued provision of special education and related services, your student will be considered a general education student and will not be entitled to any of the protections under IDEA, Does my student still graduate? Your student may still graduate and be awarded a regular high school diploma
label: VRHS ARD Specialist - FAQ's

Under IDEA, special education services must be available to an eligible student or adult student until he or she graduates with a regular high school diploma or exceeds the age eligibility requirement for special education under state law which is 21 in Texas.

text: PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information. PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information Hello Parents! Thank you for electing to receive more information about applying for accommodations with College Board for the PSAT 8/9, PSAT/NMSQT, SAT, and AP exams! Below you will find basic information and links to more detailed information. Attached you will find two forms as explained in the process below. ELIGIBILITY Some students with documented disabilities may be eligible for accommodations on College Board exams. Prior to receiving accommodations on College Board exams, requests for accommodations must be approved through College Board’s Services for Students with Disabilities (SSD). In general, students approved by SSD for College Board testing accommodations meet the criteria discussed below: 1. Student Has a Documented Disability 2. Participation in a College
label: Vista Ridge Special Education - PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information

text: PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information. Board Exam Is Impacted 3. Requested Accommodation Is Needed 4. Accommodation Is Received on School Tests FACTS TO CONSIDER • Not all students with disabilities require accommodations. Some students with disabilities who receive accommodations in school may not require accommodations on College Board exams. • The inability to finish a College Board exam in the allotted time does not equate to the student having a disability nor would that student require accommodations. • The College Board’s review process is thorough. Documentation must support both the existence of a disability and the need for the requested accommodations. • Some accommodations are administered differently on College Board exams than they are at some schools. For example, students approved for readers or scribes must test in a one- to-one setting. Students approved for extended time must stay the entire time for which they’re approved, even if they complete a section early. Therefore, students
label: Vista Ridge Special Education - PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information

text: PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information. who do not regularly use extended time on classroom tests sometimes prefer not to request it. • College Board is an outside, not-for-profit company whose exams are not considered part of a student’s education as provided by a public school district. This means that a Section 504 or ARD committee cannot add an accommodation to a student’s plan that is aimed at a College Board exam and is not appropriate for the student in the classroom on regular and routine basis. TYPICAL ACCOMMODATIONS College Board considers all reasonable requests for accommodations needed by students with documented disabilities. Available accommodations are not limited to those listed. Most commonly requested accommodations include: • Extended time • Computer use for essays • Extra and extended breaks • Reading and seeing accommodations • Four-function calculator Other accommodations in presentation, responding, timing/scheduling, and setting are available as appropriate. These can be viewed [HERE](https://www.collegeboard.org/students-with-disabilities/typical-accommodations/other) . DOCUMENTATION
label: Vista Ridge Special Education - PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information

text: PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information. REQUIREMENTS Requirements vary per disability. In order for LISD to file an accommodation request on a student’s behalf, we ask that the student has a 504 Plan/IAP or Special Education IEP with the requested accommodation in place, usually for a minimum of 4 months. Further requirements can be found [HERE](https://www.collegeboard.org/students-with-disabilities/documentation-guidelines/disability-documentation) . DECISION NOTIFICATION Most students are mailed a decision letter explaining the approved accommodations or the reasons for denial. Students with a College Board My Organizer account who are registered for the SAT can view their decision letter by signing into My Organizer. If the parent’s email is also associated with the student’s My Organizer account, the student and parent will receive an email when the decision letter is available instead of a mailed letter. Schools are also notified by email when a decision is made. Please keep in mind that the decision is made solely by College Board, not
label: Vista Ridge Special Education - PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information

text: PSAT/SAT/ACT - College Board Information. Leander ISD. PSAT/NMSQT, SAT, and AP Exams · PSAT/NMSQT is taken in October by all 10th and 11th grade students. · AP Exam(s) are taken in May by 9th – 12th graders at the conclusion of an AP course. text: VRHS ART-T. Gonzales. Find Ourselves and Lose Ourselves at the Same Time . - Thomas Merton Visual Art is an important part of a student’s education Art exercises the imagination and challenges students to think creatively and find unique solutions to various visual problems. The practice of these creative problem solving skills foster higher level thinking skills and also offers students the opportunity to work cooperatively, to be responsible, and to appreciate other cultures and the world around them. Overview of the Courses I Teach Welcome to Art I Art I is an introductory course designed to teach students to apply the elements and principles of design to the creative process. Art I students will use a variety of media, techniques, processes, and tools to demonstrate understanding of the elements of art and principles of design, awareness of aesthetic concerns, and the ability to communicate ideas through artwork. Students will critique and reflect

This course will be a survey of the American experience from the Reconstruction era (ca. 1877) to present day. Topics will include the American Industrial Revolution, Westward Expansion, Progressive Reform Movements, World War 1, the Great Depression, World War II, the Cold War, Civil Rights Movement, and social conditions of the 50's through the New Millennium. text: Resources. Resources Resources Quizlet Quizlet is a website that creates flashcards for you to study. You can play other memorization games on Quizlet and download the app to your phone. [studyspanish.com](https://studyspanish.com/) This is a great website that really breaks down grammar with clear explanations. It is well organized and offers lessons, examples, quizzes, and more. [Gimkit](https://www.gimkit.com/class/join/673e62631854ac73fbfe2a7f) Gimkit is fun way to practice you vocabulary. text: Human Growth and Development. Human Growth and Development HGD Expectations Course Description Human Growth and Development is an examination of human development across the lifespan, focusing on common physical, cognitive, emotional, and social developmental milestones from conception through death. This class is focused on equipping students with human growth and development knowledge for all stages of life. Students use these skills to promote the well-being and healthy development of children and adults. The course is generally taught as an introductory course in developmental psychology, human development, or education and training. HGD [Syllabus](https://docs.google.com/document/d/10pnLFHKrEbGXz23DRKfdYcFEIo-plJOvAWH9Ha7wBeU/edit?usp=sharing) Tutorials: Tuesday and Thursday 7:45-8:15 Lunches

text: Phillips APUSH. Phillips APUSH Phillips APUSH Brent Phillips: Brent_Phillips@leanderisd.org Welcome to APUSH! A rapid-paced, two-semester, college-level course, Advanced Placement United States History surveys the major themes and events that comprise the broad sweep of American history, from the eve of European colonization to the modern day. By design, this course is both reading and writing intensive, with students' routine use of college preparatory practices as well as historical thinking skills/methods inextricably tied to their overall success. The AP U.S. History course is designed to provide students with the skills and factual knowledge necessary to deal critically with the problems and materials in U.S. History. The program prepares students for intermediate and advanced college courses by making demands upon them equivalent to those made
label: Phillips APUSH

text: Phillips APUSH. by full-year introductory college courses. Students should learn to assess historical materials—their relevance to a given interpretive problem, reliability, and importance—and to weigh the evidence and interpretations presented in historical scholarship (From the Advanced Placement Course Description for AP United States History , published by the College Board). Primary goals of the course include developing a student’s (1) understanding of the principal themes in American history, (2) ability to analyze historical evidence, and (3) ability to analyze and to express historical understanding in writing and other forms of communication. Emphasis is placed on class discussion, the use of primary and secondary sources, critical reading, and analytical writing. Mastery of content is essential, but of equal value is the development of: * study and analytical skills * constructing and evaluating historical interpretations * critical reading of primary and secondary sources * using historical knowledge as a guide to present understanding and
label: Phillips APUSH

text: Phillips APUSH. action * making historical analogies * empathizing with the past & its people Every AP course requires hard work and an unwavering commitment to intellectual growth. All students are therefore strongly encouraged to dedicate themselves to the goals of AP U.S. History, to embrace its college-level rigor and routine, and to take the College Board Advanced Placement United States History examination at the end of the school year ( May) , which offers the possibility of earning 6 hours of college credit . Email: brent.phillips@leanderisd.org Room #- 2021, Phone Ext.# 41923 We use Google Classroom for most of our assignments. If you would like access to your child's Google Classroom account, please send me an email requesting access and I will enter your email into Google Classroom. Syllabus Syllabus Personal Financial Literacy Syllabus- Vista Ridge High School Coach Romero / Email: jr.romero@leanderisd.org Course Overview: This course focuses on a study of the way in which individuals, households, businesses, and the government participate in the operation of the economy. The primary objective of this course is to teach students the basic tool kit
label: J.R. Romero - Head Softball Coach - Syllabus

text: Syllabus. of economic concepts that will enable them to make better informed choices in the marketplace and in daily life, therefore becoming better consumers and citizens. Students study the concepts of scarcity, supply and demand, markets, business firms, competition, labor, agriculture, monopolies, government policy, and many more. Skills Utilized: Students will be expected to think critically. Assignments are designed to enhance students’ oral and written comprehension as well as communication skills. This course will use a variety of media to test and enhance these skills. Students will be expected to analyze and interpret primary documents and data (one of the primary tasks for really understanding economics) in both oral and written form. Course Objectives: Students will develop and acquire knowledge of the use of power and authority on the forces of economics. Students will develop and acquire knowledge of the role the economy has had on the development of democratic institutions.
label: J.R. Romero - Head Softball Coach - Syllabus

text: Syllabus. Students will develop and acquire knowledge of the powerful force economics has had on the world. Students will develop and acquire knowledge of how science and technology has played a key role in developmental economics. Students will research, analyze, and compare/contrast various economic systems (i.e. free market, command, traditional and mixed economies) throughout the history of the world. text: VRHS ASL - Deaf History. VRHS ASL - Deaf History Deaf History a brief history of the deaf community The history of the Deaf community is a story of resilience, advocacy, and the recognition of American Sign Language (ASL) as a rich and complete language. Over the past 200 years, Deaf individuals have worked to improve education, accessibility, and equal opportunities while preserving their language and culture. Today, ASL
label: VRHS ASL - Deaf History

text: VRHS ASL - Deaf History. is recognized as one of the most widely used languages in the United States, and Deaf culture continues to thrive. 1817 The American School for the Deaf opened in Hartford, Conneticut. It was founded by Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and Laurent Clerc, a Deaf educator from France. The school played a major role in the development of ASL. 1864 The U.S. government authorized the creation of what is now Gallaudet University in Washington, D.C. - the world's only university specifically desined for Deaf and hard of hearing students. It remains an international leader in Deaf education and research. 1960 Linguist William Stokoe published groundbreaking research showing that ASL has its own grammar and structure, proving it is a complete language rather than a system of gestures. His work changed how ASL was viewed around the world. 1988 Students at Gallaudet University organized the historic Deaf President Now (DPN) movement after a
label: VRHS ASL - Deaf History

text: VRHS ASL - Deaf History. hearing president was selected over qualified Deaf candidates. The protest led to the appointment of Dr. I. King Jordan, Gallaudet's first Deaf president, and became a defining moment in the Deaf civil rights movement. 1990 The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) became law, expanding civil rights protections and improving accessibility for individuals with disabilities, including members of the Deaf community. The momentum created by the Deaf President Now movement helped bring national attention to disability rights. why deaf history matters Understanding Deaf history helps us appreciate the challenges and achievements of the Deaf community. It reminds us that language, accessibility, and equal opportunities have been shaped by generations of advocates who worked to ensure that Deaf individuals could fully participate in education, employment, and society. As ASL students, learning this history helps us become respectful communicators and better allies to the Deaf community.
label: VRHS ASL - Deaf History

text: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette. VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette Deaf Etiquette Communicating with respect Learning ASL also means learning about Deaf culture and respectful communication. Deaf etiquette includes the customs and social norms that help create clear, respectful, and inclusive interactions. Every Deaf person has unique communication preferences, so the most important rule is to be respectful an ask what works best for the individual. 👋 getting someone's
label: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette

text: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette. attention Since Deaf individuals may not hear their name being called, there are respectful ways to get someone's attention. ✅ Appropriate Ways Give a small wave within the person's field of vision Gently tap their shoulder or upper arm Flash the room lights once or twice (when appropriate) Lightly stomp on the floor or tap a nearby table so vibrations can be felt ❌ Avoid Throwing objects Yelling louder Grabbing someone aggressively Snapping fingers directly in someone's face These visual and tactile methods are commonly used within the Deaf community. 👀 maintain eye contact Eye contact is one of the most imporant parts of ASL communication. When someone is signing: ✅ Watch the signer ✅ M aintain eye contact ✅ Stay visually engaged Looking away repeatedly while someone is signing may appear as though you are no longer paying attention, you are not interested in the conversation, rude, or there
label: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette

text: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette. is an emergency. 😊 use facial expressions In ASL, facial expressions are part of the language - not just emotions. They help communicate: Questions Emotions Emphasis Grammar Tone A blank face can change or reduce the meaning of a message. It could also alter whether a sign is signed correctly or not. 🗣️ Communicate clearly If a Deaf person is using an interpreter: ✅ Sp eak directly to the Deaf person ✅ Make eye contact with the Deaf person ❌ Do not speak to the interpreter instead The interpreter is there to facilitate communication - not participate in the conversation. ✍️ be flexible Not every Deaf person communicated the same way. Some people use: American Sign Language (ASL) Spoken English Lipreading Writing Texting Speach-to-text technology Other communication methods If you are unsure, simply ask: "How do you prefer to communicate?" Respecting someone's preferred communication method is one of the best
label: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette

text: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette. forms of Deaf etiquette. 🚫 Things to avoid Try not to: ❌ Assume every Deaf person reads lips ❌ Assume every Deaf person uses ASL ❌ Say "never mind" if communication becomes difficult ❌ Cover your mouth while speaking ❌ Turn away while communicating ❌ Interrupt someone while they are signing If communication isn't working, try rephrasing, writing it down, or using another communication method instead of giving up. 💙 Respect deaf culture The Deaf community has a rich language, history, and culture. Showing respect means: Be patient Be willing to learn Valuing ASL as a complete language Appreaciating Deaf culture and identity Including everyone in conversations Small actions can make a big difference in creating an inclusive environment. 🌟 quick etiquette checklist ✅ DO: Maintain eye contact Wave or gently tap a shoulder to get attention Speak directly to the Deaf person Use appropriate facial expressions Ask about communication
label: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette

text: VRHS ASL - Deaf Etiquette. preferences Be patient and respectful ❌ DON'T: Yell or over-enunciate Throw objects to get attention Talk only to the interpreter Assume everyone communicated the same way Give up by saying, "Never mind" Look away while someone is signing did you know? 🤟 Eye contact is an essential part of ASL because signers communicate visually, not auditorily. 💡 Flashing the lights or gently tapping someone's shoulder are culturally accepted ways to get a Deaf person's attention. 🧏 Not all Deaf people use ASL or lipread - communication preferences vary from person to person. Mrs. Saler-sanchez's reminder Respect is the foundation of communication. Learning Deaf etiquette helps us become not only better ASL students but also thoughtful, respectful communicators who value the language, culture, and experiences of the Deaf community.

text: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts. VRHS ASL - ASL Facts ASL Facts 💡did you know? 💡 American Sign Language (ASL) is one of the most widely used languages in the United States! While many people think ASL is simply, "English with hand signs," it is actually a complete language with its own grammar, history, and culture. Explore some fun facts below to learn more about this incredible language. ❌myth❌
label: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts

text: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts. ASL is just English with hand signs Everyone in the world uses the same sign language Deaf people can all lipread Fingerspelling is the entire language ASL is only for Deaf people ✅fact✅ ASL has its own grammar and sentence structure Every country may have its own sign language Many Deaf people do not rely on lipreading, and communication preferences vary Fingerspelling is only one small part of ASL Deaf, hard of hearing, and hearing people all use ASL ❓why learn ASL ❓ Learning ASL is about much more than learning signs. It helps students: Build communication skills Develop cultural awareness Connect with the Deaf community Strengthen visual learning and observation skills Become more inclusive and empathetic communicators Every new sign is another step toward understanding a language, a culture, and a community. 🌎 Sign language is not universal 🌎 Many people are surprised to learn that there isn't just
label: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts

text: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts. one sign language. Different countries have their own sign languages, including: American Sign Language (ASL) British Sign Language (BSL) French Sign Language (LSF) Japanese Sign Language (JSL) Australian Sign Language (Auslan) Just like spoken languages, sign languages developed independently around the world. 🤟 asl is a real language 🤟 ASL is a complete and antural language with its own grammar, sentence structure, and vocabulary. It is not simply English translated into signs. 🇺🇲 asl is one of the most used languages in the U.s. 🇺🇲 American Sign Language is among the most commonly used languages in the United States and is used by hundred of thousands of Deaf, hard of hearing, and hearing individuals every day. 🌟 asl is constantly growing 🌟 Like spoken langauge, ASL changes over time. New signs are created as technology, culture, and society evolve. Different regions may also have unique signs for the same concept.
label: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts

text: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts. 🎓 asl can count toward graduation 🎓 Many high schools and colleges recognize ASL as a world language, allowing students to fulfill language graduation requirements while learning about Deaf culture. 🖐️ every sign has 5 parameters 🖐️ Every ASL sign is made up of five important parts: Handshape Palm Orientation Location Movement Non-manual markers/morphemes (Facial expressions & Body Language) Changing just one of these can change the meaning of a sign. 👀 asl is a visual language 👀 Instead of relying on sound, ASL uses: Hands Face Eyes Body Movement Space This is why eye contact is so important during conversations. 😁 your face is part of the language 😁 In ASL, facial expressions are not optional. They communicate: Questions Emotions Grammar Emphasis Tone Without facial expressions, the meaning of a sentence can completely change. 📖 asl has its own grammar 📖 ASL does not follow English word order. label: VRHS ASL - ASL Facts

In reality, fingerspelling is mainly used for: Names Places Brand names Words without established signs Most everyday conversations use signs rather than spelling every word. 🧏 hearing people use asl too 👂 ASL is used by: Deaf individuals Hard of hearing individuals Hearing family members Teachers Interpreters Medical professionals First responders Students Friends od the Deaf community Learning ASL helps connect people across different communities. 🏆 mrs. saler-sanchez's fun challenge 🏅 How many of these fun facts surprised you? Before submitting your video, review the guidelines below: Video & Deaf Culture Guidelines: Maintain eye contact (or eye gaze) When signing, look at your communication partner (the camera), not at your hands. When you are signing a story and it has multiple characters, make sure you are also maintaining eye gaze in the story as if those people are talking to eachother. Eye contact shows respect, engagement, confidence, and active communication. Remember: In ASL, your eyes and facial expressions are part of the conversation. Make sure your hands do not leave the camera frame, your arms are not blocked, your face remains visible, and your signing space can be seen clearly. Sign languages rely on hand movements, facial expressions, and body positioning to communicate meaning, so the entire signing space needs to be visible. Dress for Success Wear clothing that allows your signing to be easily seen. Reccommended: ✅ Solid-colored shirt ✅ Colors that contrast with your skin tone ✅ Hair pulled away from your face (if needed) ✅ Minimal distractions Avoid: ❌ Busy patterns ❌ Clothing that blends into your hands ❌ Large jewelry that distracts from signing (this is also dangerous) ❌ Hats or anything covering your face Solid clothing and strong contrast improve visibility of the hands and face. text: About Coach Sim. About Coach Sim About Coach Sim 2026-2027 is my 23rd year of teaching and coaching in Texas and my 12th year at Vista Ridge. My teaching and coaching career has taken me to several different places and allowed me to teach and coach many different subjects, sports, and students. I taught AP Calculus AB at Round Rock Stony Point for 3 years, and am in my eleventh year of teaching Calculus at Vista Ridge. I have been a reader for the AP Calculus BC exam for 6 years. Calculus is a very exciting content, and I am thrilled to be able to teach Calculus at Vista Ridge. I am from a family of educators where I learned from an early
label: VRHS: Coach Sim's Calculus Site - About Coach Sim

text: About Coach Sim. age the value of education. Through the passion I bring to the classroom everyday, I hope to instill a love of learning as well as inspire my students to value mistakes as just another way to learn and grow. While math may be my subject of expertise, I love teaching because I love working with students, and I value the opportunity to help them achieve their goals and encourage them down their own path. I love being a part of the Vista Ridge family of Rangers and am excited about the 2026-2027 year! The 2026 cohort of AP Calclus BC students at VRHS were exceptionally successful on the AP Exam. 100% of students sat for the AP Exam and 92% (106/115) received a recommended score of 3 or higher. Of those students 77 (67%) earned a 5! This is an incredible accomplishment and this group worked extremely hard to earn
label: VRHS: Coach Sim's Calculus Site - About Coach Sim

text: About Coach Sim. these exceptional scores. In 2025, 100% of students sat for the exam and 96% (108/112) received a recommended score of 3 or higher. Of those students 86 (77%) earned a 5! The 2024 AP Calculus BC VRHS cohort received stellar scores with 100% of students sitting for the exam and 92% (81/88) receiving a recommended score of 3 or higher. Out of those scores, 56 students (64%) earned a 5. The 2023 testing group saw 88% of BC students (69/77) earn a 3 or higher with 48 students (62%) earning a 5. The data shown above is only part of the narrative , but we truly believe we are preparing students for their next steps after high school by engaging in college level content, but also learning how to problem solve and collaborate more effectively. This class is just as much about learning time management, how to work in teams,
label: VRHS: Coach Sim's Calculus Site - About Coach Sim

text: Mrs. Tudtud - VRHS Chemistry Mrs. Tudtud In Chemistry, students conduct laboratory and field investigations, use scientific practices during investigations, and make informed decisions using critical thinking and scientific problem solving. Students study a variety of topics that include characteristics of matter, use of the Periodic Table, development of atomic theory, chemical bonding, chemical stoichiometry, gas laws, solution chemistry, acid-base chemistry, thermochemistry, and nuclear chemistry. Students investigate how chemistry is an integral part of our daily lives. By the end of Grade 12, students are expected to gain sufficient knowledge of the scientific and engineering practices across the disciplines of science to make informed decisions using critical thinking and scientific problem solving . text: MR. TYLER - Money Matters. MR. TYLER - Money Matters Money Matters Money Matters is a practical course designed to help students develop the skills needed to make smart financial decisions. Students will learn how to manage money, set short- and long-term financial goals, and evaluate financial choices based on their individual needs. Students will explore budgeting, saving, investing, taxes, credit, insurance, risk management, retirement planning, and other real-world financial topics. The goal is to give students the knowledge and confidence to make informed financial decisions throughout their lives. [Syllabus](https://drive.google.com/file/d/16Pm9U4IHrXTOxfKkppmd5twR4NJAfNUj/view?usp=sharing) [Year at a Glance](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1a7-9cGj2u_PEGemJoAnJHlD2MNwPGA9miUMtJsu5-i4/edit?usp=sharing)

text: MR. TYLER - Algebraic Reasoning. MR. TYLER - Algebraic Reasoning Algebraic Reasoning Algebraic Reasoning helps students strengthen their understanding of algebra and functions while developing problem-solving and critical-thinking skills. Students will explore linear, quadratic, exponential, absolute value, and other types of functions through equations, graphs, tables, and real-world situations. Throughout the course, students will learn to recognize patterns, analyze relationships, use technology, and apply mathematics to solve problems. The goal is to build both mathematical confidence and reasoning skills that students can use in future classes, college, and the workplace. By Curtis Locklear

Whenever we meet a challenge,
the Rangers will stand tall.
We’ll set our hearts to the task,
each victory’s for us all.

To the runner goes the glory,
though the race be hard and long.
We’ll build our lives on all that’s right,
stand fast against all wrong.

keep each promise that is made.
The pride that’s in the Ranger Star,
shines bright and never fades.

As the years go by,
for the red, black and silver,
for the glory, Vista Ridge High.

text: From the linked document Cap Decorating Guidelines: VRHS Senior Cap Decorating Guidelines Please take into consideration the following rules when decorating your graduation cap. Failure to follow these rules will result in the removal of the cap before the ceremony. * No objects such as signs, stuffed animals, bells, flowers, or any 3D object may rest on the cap. * ALL decorations MUST lay FLAT on the cap. * Nothing can lay perpendicular thus allowing us to see the decoration beyond eye level. * Nothing can hang down from any side of the cap. * Your cap CANNOT make noise. * No bells, horns, or anything that makes noise. * Designs must not be inappropriate or privilege will be taken away. * Designs may not include: * Offensive language, flags * Double meaning words * Nicknames (unless approved) * Gang-related signs/slang * Negative or rude language * Boyfriend or Girlfriend’s name * Political affiliation * Alcohol, drugs,
label: Cap Decorating Guidelines

Submission Is Missing for Attendance

IMPORTANT NOTE: The Submission Is Missing for Attendance Notification is set as a Mandatory
notification. Therefore, all scheduled teachers will receive a Notification, on their Notification page
when the Attendance Missing Submission report is run by office personnel. In order to set this up,
teachers must modify the settings in their grade book, as described in the following document.

Adding a Notification Subscription

1) Select Notification Subscriptions located under your
employee ID# on your home TAC screen.

2) You will now see this:

There are several subscription options you can choose from. Let’s look at the choices available to you.
Do Not Subscribe – Select this option if you do not want to receive notifications for the corresponding
notification type.
Subscribe – Select this option to only get notifications in TAC.
label: Notification Subscription in TAC (Notification Subscriptions in TAC)

From the linked document LISD Stadium Info (Stadium Rules & Regulations): Leander ISD Stadium Rules & Regulations

A.C. Bible, John Gupton, Ed W. Monroe Stadiums

1. Gates will open sixty minutes before game time.

2. No outside food or drinks are allowed into the stadium.

3. Leander ISD Regional Stadiums are clear bag only facilities.

4. Alcoholic beverages, tobacco products (including e-cigs), drugs and weapons of any sort are prohibited by law
from the stadium.

5. General Admission Tickets only provide admission to the stadium. They do not provide a seat. Seating for general
admission is first come, first served.

6. Patrons who leave the stadium for any reason must purchase another ticket to re -enter. This includes patrons
with any type of pass. Exceptions for medical emergencies only.

7. Animals are not allowed in the stadium. Service animals are allowed with proper credentials.
label: LISD Stadium Info (Stadium Rules & Regulations)

text:
From the linked document LISD Stadium Info (Stadium Rules & Regulations): 8. No airborne material or devices (ex. drones) of any kind unless approved by the athletic office and the campus.

9. No ice chests allowed in stadium except for teams and support groups.

10. Athletic equipment (any type of ball, bats, skateboard, bicycle, frisbees, scooters, rollerblades, etc.) is prohibited
in the stadium.

11. Only credentialed, authorized personnel are allowed on the field and in the press box.

12. Volunteers (band, cheer, tunnel crews) must return to the stands after helping their group.

13. No Bluetooth speakers, cannons, train horns, artificial noisemakers, laser pointers, smoke machines, powder or
confetti allowed.

14. Spirit signs must be positive in nature. Signs are not allowed to be taped to any part of the stadium. Signs may be
posted on the railing with zip ties. Signs and zip ties must be removed and properly disposed of immediately
following the conclusion of the game.
label: LISD Stadium Info (Stadium Rules & Regulations)

text:
From the linked document LISD Stadium Info (Stadium Rules & Regulations): 15. Private tailgating is not allowed.

16. Teams or spectators are not allowed to have “smoke bombs” or “grenades” of any type.

17. Leander ISD does not allow patrons or businesses to hand out literature or promotional items without prior
consent. This covers all school property including parking lots. For example, policy does not permit flyers to be
handed out or placed on windshields. The district also prohibits the distribution of promotional items inside or
outside the stadium with the exception of Leander ISD sponsors and pre-approved organizations.
label: LISD Stadium Info (Stadium Rules & Regulations)

Welcome to Leander Independent School District!
As parents and students, you have an interest in the policies and procedures that govern the schools
of the District. Policies are established to create an orderly, friendly, learning environment for each
student.

This handbook contains a great deal of required and useful information for students and parents. It
cannot be as personal as we would like. Therefore, we address students, not directly as "you," but
rather as "the student," "student," or "children." The term "the student's parent" may refer to the
parent, legal guardian, or another person who has agreed to assume responsibility for the student.

Decision-Making
The quality of life at school depends on the decisions students make. If they make good decis ions, then they can avoid
troublesome situations at home, at school, or with friends. Making decisions can often be difficult because others may try
to talk our children into doing something wrong. They may dare them, tease them, or even call them names if they don’t go
along with the crowd. Students can use this four -step formula for making responsible decisions. Stop, Think, Evaluate,
Proceed.
● STOP. Take time to look around you. Know where you are and who is with you. Stand straight. Appear selfconfident. Look the other person in the eye.
label: 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English)

text:
From the linked document 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English): ● THINK. To think clearly: Listen carefully to what the other person is saying. Hear what is being suggested to you
or asked of you. Realize whether the situation or suggestion has the potential for trouble.
● EVALUATE. What will the consequences of my actions be? Ask yourself: Will I cause someone else to get hurt or
to get into trouble? Will my action break a school rule? Will my action break a law? What GOOD things can
happen? What BAD things can happen? Is it worth it in the long run?
● PROCEED. Respond or act in a way that will avoid the trouble. Remove yourself from the situation. Leave.
Change the subject. Make another suggestion. Ignore what was said or suggested. Make a joke of it. Say:
“Friends don’t ask friends to do something that will get them into trouble.” Say NO! You are important. There is
label: 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English)

text:
From the linked document 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English): only one of you in the whole world. You don’t need to wait for others to make your decisions for you. If you think
you are right and try to be honest and fair, you will probably choose the right way to act. You are the one who can
make your school days happy days.

Self-Discipline
One important lesson students learn i n school is self -discipline. Self -discipline is the key to good conduct and proper
consideration for other people. For those who do not exercise self -discipline, the following alternatives may be
used/assigned by school officials:
● Community Service - a task assigned as a result of failure to show respect for people or property.
● Counseling - a conference with a teacher, counselor, or principal.
● Withdrawal of Privileges - a time apart from classmates for a portion of a day or more.
label: 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English)

text:
From the linked document 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English): ● Parent Conference - a discussion with the student, his/her parents, the teacher, a counselor, and/or the principal.
● Detention - a time apart from classmates assigned during lunch, or before/after school. Parents will be notified.
● Suspension - a serious disciplinary measure that results in the loss of the privilege of attending class or school for
a designated time period.
● Alternative Education - a placement in the Leander Extended Opportunity Center (LEO). This is a highly
structured environment for students who are not experiencing success in the regular classroom.
● Expulsion - a serious disciplinary measure resulting in the loss of the privilege of attending a LISD school and
placement at a juvenile detention center school for a time period.
● Judicial Proceeding - a legal measure that may be taken if necessary.
● Peer Mediation - a conflict resolution approach to problem solving between students.

Homework
When a teacher assigns homework, it is to provide additional practice for lessons already taught and to build good study
habits. Students are encouraged to always complete homework assignments to the very best of their ability.

Purpose of Homework
● To improve achievement.
● To nurture the development of good study habits.
label: 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English)

text:
From the linked document 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English): ● To familiarize parents with their child(ren)’s work and give parents a chance for involvement.
● To provide more time for in-class instruction.

Guidelines Teachers Follow in Assigning Homework
● Students should have prior instruction.
● Homework should be directly related to classroom instruction.
● The purpose of homework should be clearly identified and articulated to the student.
● Homework should be promptly reviewed and returned to the student with descriptive feedback.
● Teachers should consider the availability of resources at home before assigning homework.
● Assignments should take no more than the "suggested time frame" to complete.

What Students Are Expected To Do
● Promptly inform parents of the homework assignment.
● Make an effort to understand the assignment.
● Make a consistent effort to complete the assignment.
● Take responsibility for turning in the assignment.

The FAFSA is an online application that should be com pleted during a student’s senior year in high school. Completing a
FAFSA may qualify a student for federal student loans, grants, the work -study program, scholarships, and student/parent
loans (subsidized & unsubsidized). Additionally, many universities re quire the FAFSA to be filled out to be eligible for

● Permanent U.S. resident with an Alien Registration Card (I-551)

● Eligible noncitizen with an Arrival/Departure Record (I -94) showing you as a: (a) Refugee (b) Asylum granted (c)
Parolee (d) Cuban-Haitian entrant. Additional information can be found at https://fafsa.ed.gov/.

Please note that guidance provided that includes, but is not limited to, illness or presence of illness may be subject to

Clinic Overview
Leander ISD is committed to providing a healthy, safe, and ready-to-learn environment for all students. Each campus
clinic is staffed by a licensed nurse who provides professional school health services in accordance with applicable law,
nursing standards, and District procedures. Some campuses also have the support of a Clinic Health Aide, who works
under the direction of the campus nurse to assist with routine clinic operations and student health needs.

The Health Services Department partners with a local licensed physician who provides medical oversight, develops and

Department as needed.

The campus clinic supports students who become ill or injured during the school day, require medication administration or
other authorized health-related services, or need assistance managing a documented health condition while at school.
Clinic services are intended to support student health, safety, and access to instruction and do not replace routine medical
care provided by a student’s family or healthcare provider.

The campus clinic is not the appropriate place for monitoring students who need a “brain break” or to sit out of P.E./recess.
This is due to unnecessary exposure to illness, emergencies, and the need to maintain confidentiality.

LISD recognizes the importance of partnering with parents/guardians to ensure a healthy environment for all our students

Bullying is defined in state law as a sing le significant act or a pattern of acts by one or more students directed at another
student that exploits an imbalance of power and involves engaging in written or verbal expression, expression through
electronic means, or physical conduct that:
● Has the effect or will have the effect of physically harming a student, damaging a student’s property, or placing a
student in reasonable fear of harm to the student’s person or of damage to the student’s property;
● Is sufficiently severe, persistent, or pervasive that the action or threat creates an intimidating, threatening, or
abusive educational environment for a student;
● Materially and substantially disrupts the educational process or the orderly operation of a classroom or school; or
label: 26-27 LISD Student & Parent Handbook (Student Handbook - English)

Bullying includes cyberbullying. Cyberbullying is defined in state law as bullying that is done through the use of any
electronic communication device, including through the use of:
● A cellular or other type of telephone
● A computer
● A camera
● Electronic mail
● Instant messaging
● Text messaging
● A social media application
● An internet website
● Any other internet-based communication tool.

Bullying is prohibited by the district and could include:
● Hazing
● Threats
● Taunting
● Teasing
● Confinement
● Assault
● Demands for money
● Destruction of property
● Theft of valued possessions
● Name-calling
● Rumor-spreading
● Ostracism

include an explanation of how the information in the record is inaccurate. If the District denies the request to amend the
records, the parent or eligible student has the right to request a hearing. If the records are not amended as a result of the
hearing, the parent or eligible student has 30 school days to exercise the right to place a statement commenting on the
